Stage 3 · Reading

The world’s funniest joke was nobody’s favourite

Two million ratings, seventy countries, and what actually stops a joke crossing a border.

😂🌐
1 · Before you read. When a comedy from another country does not make you laugh, what is usually missing?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The world’s funniest joke was nobody’s favourite

Written for this course, from the LaughLab experiment run by the psychologist Richard Wiseman with the British Association for the Advancement of Science, 2001–2002.

1In 2001 a British psychologist put a website online and invited the world to submit jokes and rate other people’s. Over the following year he collected around forty thousand jokes and close to two million ratings from more than seventy countries, each rating given on a five-point scale that the project called, inevitably, the Giggleometer. An experiment like that only works if enough people join in, and they will not join in unless taking part costs them almost nothing; a five-second click was the whole design. It remains one of the largest experiments on humour ever attempted.

2The winner was a short, well-built joke about two hunters, one of whom misunderstands an emergency operator with fatal results. It is neat rather than hilarious, and the researcher was honest about why it won: it did not top anybody’s personal list, but almost nobody rated it distasteful. A joke can win a worldwide vote provided that it offends no one, which is a different achievement from being funny. Unless a competition is designed to reward strong reactions, it will reward inoffensiveness instead.

3The national patterns were more interesting than the winner. Raters in Britain, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand tended to prefer wordplay — a witty final line that turns on a double meaning. Americans and Canadians more often chose jokes in which one person is made to look ridiculous by another. Several continental European groups favoured the surreal, and jokes about illness and death that other raters found faintly distasteful. Germans, who are routinely accused of having no sense of humour at all, gave high ratings across the widest range of joke types of anyone in the study. These are tendencies rather than rules: a preference only counts as a pattern if thousands of people share it, and even if they do, plenty of individuals inside every group will disagree.

4None of that describes a nation, and it would be irritating to pretend otherwise. Anybody who volunteers to spend an evening rating jokes on a website in 2001 is, by definition, an unusual person, and the sample selected itself. Unless you can draw people at random, you are describing the visitors to one website rather than a country. The finding is real as long as it is stated that carefully, and pointless the moment somebody turns it into a claim about national character.

5What the experiment could not measure is the thing that actually stops comedy at borders. A joke is not funny unless you know which rule is being broken, and the rule is usually local. A long silence is hilarious in a country where people do not interrupt each other, and merely tedious where they do. A character who cannot say what he means is comical to one audience and simply annoying to another, which keeps waiting for a punchline that the writers never intended to supply, and which comes away finding the whole performance predictable rather than thought-provoking.

6Some things travel anyway. Physical comedy survives almost everywhere, as long as the situation is clear within about five seconds. So does the absurd, provided that it is played completely straight: a ridiculous premise performed by actors behaving as though it were entirely normal seems to work on every audience anybody has tried it on. What does not survive is anything built on a specific social rule, unless the viewer already holds it, and no amount of subtitling will install it. The remakes that succeed keep the shape and rewrite the rule; the ones that fail translate the rule faithfully and wonder why the room is quiet.

Text A · Two million ratings

Unless a competition is designed to reward strong reactions, it will reward inoffensiveness instead.

Text B · The rule you have to know already

Written for this course.

None of that describes a nation, and it would be irritating to pretend otherwise. Anybody who volunteers to spend an evening rating jokes on a website in 2001 is, by definition, an unusual person, and the sample selected itself. Stage 4 · Conditions beyond if

Unless, as long as, provided that, in case

All of them set a condition. Each one sets a different kind, and two of them are regularly used to mean the opposite of what the speaker intended.

Two traps. One: unless already contains the negative, so unless you don’t know means the opposite of what most people intend. Two: in case is not if: take an umbrella if it rains means look outside first; take an umbrella in case it rains means take it now.

4 · One idea, six conditions.
It works if the actors play it straight.  →  neutral.
It does not work unless they play it straight.  →  if not.
It works as long as they play it straight.  →  only on that condition.

1 · Read the explanation.
Conditional conjunctions

The shape stays the same. All of these words behave like if: the condition clause takes a present tense even when the meaning is future, and the main clause carries will, an imperative or a modal. As long as you book early, it will be cheap. Never as long as you will book.

Unless = if not. The verb after it stays positive: I will not go unless she comes = I will not go if she does not come. Because the negative is already inside the word, unless she doesn’t come means something quite different and is almost always an error.

As long as and provided (that). Both mean only on this condition and are stronger than if. Provided that is the formal one, common in contracts and reviews; providing is a slightly softer version of the same thing; as long as is the everyday one. That can be dropped.

In case is a precaution, not a condition. I will take an umbrella if it rains — I check first, then decide. I will take an umbrella in case it rains — I take it now, because it might. This is one of the most frequent errors at B2.

Even if and whether or not. These say the condition makes no difference: I would watch it even if it were terrible; He will remake it whether or not it sells.

Position and commas. The condition can come first or second. When it comes first, use a comma: Unless you know the rule, it is not funny. When it comes second, no comma is needed: It is not funny unless you know the rule.

The commonest errors at this level
  • unless you don’t come — a double negative.
  • as long as it will rain — no will in the condition clause.
  • Take an umbrella if it rains when you mean in case.
  • provided to or provided of — the word is provided (that).
  • Missing the comma when the condition comes first.

Two things to watch

1 — Test unless by rewriting it with if not. If the result is a double negative, the sentence is wrong.

2 — In case looks forward from now. If you would do the thing before knowing, it is in case; if you would wait and see, it is if.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Choosing the right conjunction

The idea: the series is worth watching, but only for people who have seen the original.

Step 1 — is the condition positive or negative? Positive: they must have seen it. So if, as long as or provided that, not unless.

Step 2 — how strong is it? It is the only condition, so use a strong one: It is worth watching, as long as you have seen the original.

Step 3 — the negative version. The same idea with unless flips the main clause: It is not worth watching unless you have seen the original. Note the positive verb after unless.

Step 4 — a precaution is something else. Watch the original first, in case the remake spoils the ending — you do it now, because that might happen.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Six ways of setting a condition

if — neutral: It works if they play it straight. unless — means if not, and therefore takes a positive verb: It is not funny unless you know the rule · I will not go unless she comes. unless she doesn’t come is a double negative and says the opposite.

as long as and provided (that) mean only on this condition, and the difference between them is register: It is cheap as long as you book early in speech, They agreed, provided that the name was changed in writing. Providing (that) sits between the two, and the that is often dropped.

in case — not a condition at all but a precaution taken now because something might happen: Record it in case they cut the ending. Compare Record it if they cut the ending, which means you wait and only record afterwards. This pair is the one that separates B2 from B1.

When the condition changes nothing

even if concedes the condition and says it makes no difference: I would watch it even if it were terrible. The were is the unreal form, and it marks the condition as hypothetical. whether or not covers both possibilities at once: He will remake it whether or not it sells — and it needs no comma.

Word order and punctuation: the conditional clause can come first or second. When it comes first, a comma follows it: Unless you know the rule, it is not funny. When it comes second, no comma: It is not funny unless you know the rule.

Tense: after all of these, English uses the present for a future condition, never will: as long as you book early, not as long as you will book. The exception is the unreal condition after even if, which takes a past form: even if it were terrible.

Errors to watch: unless she doesn’t come → unless she comes · as long as you will book early → you book · Take an umbrella if it rains when you mean the precaution → in case it rains · provided that if the name changes → one conjunction is enough.

A review with conditions attached

1 · Read the model review.
Model · a review in four paragraphs

This is a six-part comedy about a family firm that repairs clocks nobody owns any more, and it is witty rather than hilarious. I laughed out loud four times in three hours, smiled almost continuously, and would recommend it to most people, as long as they are told in advance what kind of thing it is.

The premise is ridiculous and everybody plays it entirely straight, which is where the comedy comes from. The dialogue is exact: two characters spend a whole episode failing to say one obvious sentence to each other, and the writing trusts you to notice. Nothing is explained. There is no laugh track, and the pauses that would be irritating in a studio sitcom are the best thing in it here.

The middle two episodes are tedious, and I would defend them anyway. The plot stops moving for roughly forty minutes while the family argue about a bill, and the last episode does not work unless you have sat through that, because the argument is what makes the final scene thought-provoking rather than merely sad. The ending is predictable, provided that you were paying attention in episode one; if you were not, it lands as a surprise, and several reviewers who clearly were not have called it clumsy.

Do not start it unless you can watch it slowly. Anybody who wants a punchline every ninety seconds will find it pointless, and one scene in the fourth episode will strike some viewers as distasteful, whether or not that was the intention. Everybody else should watch it, in case it is not renewed.
